docs.title: Preface to the First Edition
docs.text:
What can be more tedious than the Veda, and yet what can be mort interesting, if once we know that iv is the first word spoken by the Aryan man ?"

“ The Veda has a two-fold interest : it belongs to the history of the world and to the history of India......... As long as man continues to take an interest in the history of his race, and as long as we collect in libraries and museums the relics of former ages, the first place in that long row of books which contains the records of she Aryan branch of mankind, will belong for ever to the Rig-veda." F. Mox MULLER.

THIS work is an attempt to bring within easy reach of all readers of English a translation of the Hymns of the Rigveda which, while aiming especially at close fidelity to the letter and the spirit of the original, shall be as readable and intelligible as the nature of the subject and other circumstances permit.

Veda, meaning literally knowledge, is, the name give to certain ancient works which formed the foundation of the eaxly religious belief of the Hindus. These are the Rigveda, the Sâmaveda, the Yajurveda, and the Atharvaveda ; and of these the Rigveda-—so called because its Sanhitâ or collection of mantras or hymns consists of Richas or verses intended for loud recitation--is the oldest, the most important, and the most generally interesting, some of its hymns bring rather Indo-European than Hindu, and representing the conditign of the Aryaps beford their final settlement in India. These, four Vedas are considered to be of divine crigin and to have existed from all eternity, the Rislâs or sacred poety to whom the hytnns are ascribed being merely inspired seers who saw or received them by, sight directly from the Suprgme Creator. In accordance with this belief these sacred books have been preserved and hâuded down with the most reverential care from generation to generation, and have accompanied the great army of Aṅyan immigPants in their twward march from the Land of the SeveneRivers tose Indian Ocean and the Bay'of Bengal. Each of these four Vedas is divided into two distinct parts, one the Mantra containing prayer and praise, the other the Brâhmana containing d tailed directiogs for the performance of the ceremonies at which the Mantras were to be used, and explanations of tue legends connected stb them, the whole forming a vast body of sacred literature in verse and in prose, devotional, ceremonial, expository and theosophic.

The Śanhitâ of the Rigveda is a collection of hymns and songs brought by the remote ancestors of the present Hindus from therr ancient homes on the banks of the Indus where they had been first used in adoration of the Father of Heaven, of the Sun, of Dawn, of, Agni or the God of fire, in prayers for health, wealth, lang life, offspring, cattle, victory in battle, and freedom from the bonds of smn: and celebration of the ever-renewed warfare between the beneficent thunder-wielding Indra, the special champion of the Aryans, and the malevolent powers 'of darkness and the defrons of drought who withheld the rain of heaven. = Of these hymns there are more than a thousand, arranged in ten Maṇdalas, Circles, or Books, in accordance with an ancient tradition of what we should call authorship, the hymns ascribed to the same Rishi, inspired poet or seer, or to the same school or family of Rishis being placed together. Within these divisions the hymng are generally arranged more or fess in the order of the deities to whom they are gddressed. Agni and Indra a%e the Gods mogt frequently invoked. Hymns to Agni generally re first; next comgpthose Śdd: essed to Indga, and after them those in honour Gu deitigs or derfie® objects of adoration. The ninth Book is devoted almost eikirelg to Soma, the deified juice used in pouring libations to the Gods, and the tenth forms a sort of appendix of pecutiagand miscellaneous materials. Independently of the evidence afforded by Indian tradition, there can be no rea. sonable doubt of the great antiquity of the Rigveda Sanhitâ which, wh the eaception of the Egyptian monumental records and papyrug rolls, and the recently discovered Assyrign literstu. re, is probably the oldest literary document in existence. But seems impossible to fix, with ar'ything approsching, to certainty, any date for the composition of the hymns. In the first Hymn of Book I. ancient and recent or modern Rishis or seers are spoken of, and there is other internal evidence that some hymns ¹aragguch older than others. Colbrooke came to the conclusion, from astronomical calculations, that a certain Vedic calendar Was composed in the fourteenth century before the Christian era; from which it would follow, that as this calendar must have been prepared after the arrangement of the Rigveda and the inclusion of the most modern hymn, the date of the earliest hymn might be carried back, perhaps, soute thousand years. The correctress of Colebrooke's conclusions, however, has been questioned, and some recent scholars consider that his calculations arc of a very vague character, and do not yield any such definite date. In the absence of any direct evidence, the opinions of scholars vary and must continue to vary with regard to the age of tle Hymns of the Rigveda. "The reasons, however," (to quot Professor Weber*) “by which we are fully justified in regardiag the lijerature of India as the most ancient literature of wlich written records on an extensive scale have been handed dovn to us are these :-In the more ancient parts of the Rigveda Sanhitâ, we find the Indian race settled on the north-westrrn borders of India, in the Panjâb, and even beyond the Parjâb, on the Kubhâ, or in Kabul, The gradual spread of the race from these seats towards the east, beyond the Sarasvati and over Ilindustân as far as the Ganges, can be traced in the later portions of the, Vedic writings almost step by step. The writings of the following period, that of the epic, consist of ackounss of the internal conflicts among the conquerors of Hindustâṇ themselves,

% The History of Indian Iiterature, by Albreght, Weber, Trubner's Oriental Series. 1878. : ¹ as for instance, the Mahâbhârata ; or of the Yartheypread of Brâhmanism towards the south, as, for instance, the Râmâyana. Itwve connect with this the first fairly Śecurate iffformation about India which We have from a Greek source, viz , from Megasthenes," it becomes clear that at the time of this writer the Brahmanising of Hindustân was already completed, while at the time of the Periplus (see Lassen, I. 4x., ii. 150, n ; I. Śt, ii. 192) the very southern-most point of the Dekhan had already become the scat of the worship of the wife of (iva. What a series of years, of centuries, must necessarily have elapsed before this boundless tract of country, inhabited by wild and vigorous tribes, could have been brought over to brahmanism !"

I must beg wy European readers not to expect to find in these hymns and songs the sublime poetry that they meet with in Isaiah or Job or the Psalms of David To me," says Professor Wilson, ['the verses of the Veda, except in their rhythm, and in a ess passages, appear singularly prosaic for so early an era as thai of their probable comp sition, and at any rate their chief value les not in their fancy but in their facts, social and religious." Ppfessor Cowell, also, says : "The poetry of the Rigvedl is sing (larly dgficient in that simplicity and natural pathos or sublimity which we naturally look for in the songs of an early period of Heston The language and style of most of the hymns is siigularly nrtificial..... Occasionally we meet with fine outburst, of poetry, especially in the hymns addressed to the dawn, but these are never long sustained, and as a rule we find few grand similes or metaphors." The worst fault of all, in the Collection regarded-as a whole, is the intolerable monetony of a great (umber of the hymns, a monotony which reaches its climax in up ninth Book which cgnsists. almost entirely of invocations of Soma Pavamâa, or the deified Soma juice in process of Śtraining and pugification. The great interest of x ³ Who as qmbassador of Seleucus resided for some time at the oourt of Chandragupta. Mis reporty are preserved to us chiefly in the of Arrian who lived in the second cbntury A. D. the Rigveda is, in fact, historical rather than goctical... As in its original language we see the roots and shoots of the languages of Greek and Latin, of Kelr, Teuton and Slavonian, so the deities, the myths, and the religious beliefs and practices of the Veda throw a flood of light upon the religions of all European countries before the introduction of Christianity. As the science of comparative philology could hardly have existed without the study of Sanskrit, so the comparative history of the religions of the world would have been impossible without the study of the Veda.

My translation, which follows the text of Max Miiller's splendid six-volume edition, is partly based on the work of the great scholiast Sâyana who was Prime Minister at the court of the King of Vijayanagar—in what is now the Madras District of Bellary—in the fourteenth century of our era: SŚâyana's Commentary has been consulted and carefully considered for Yhe general sense of every verse and for the meaning of every word, and his interpretation has been followed whenever it seemed rational, and consisteat with the context, and with other pasqages in which the same word or words occur. With regard to Sâyana's qualifications as an interpreter of the Veda there is, or was, a conflict of opinion among European scholars. Professor Wilson—whose translation of the Rigveda is rather a version of Sâyaṇa's paraphrase—was firmly persuaded that he had a “knowledge of his text far beyond the pretensions of any European scholar, and must have been in possession of all the interpretations which had been perpetuated by tṅaditional teaching from the carlicst times." Yet, as Dr. J. Muir has pointed out, Professor Wilson in the notes to his trraslation admits that he “occasionally failed to find in 'SAyaṇa a perfectly satisfactory guide," that “the scholiast is evidently puzzled," and thar his explanations are obscure. On the other hand Professor Rotk—the âuthor of the Vedic portion of the great St. Petcrsburg Lexicon—says in his preface to that work: "so far as regards one of the branches of Vetic literature, the treatises on theology and worship, we can dire no better guides than these commentators, so exact in all respects, who followStheir texts word by word, who, so long as even the semblance of a misconception might arise, are never weary of repeating what they have frequently said before, and who often appear as if they had been writing for us foreigners rather than for their own priestly alumni who had grown up.in the midst of these conceptions and impressions. Here...... they are in their proper ground. The case, however, is quite different when the same men assume the tak of interprating the ancient collections of hymns... Here were requircd not only quite different qualifications for interpretation but also a greater freedom of judgment and a greater breadth of view and of historical intuitions. Freedom of judgment, however, was wanting to priestly learning, whilst in India no one has ever had any conceptien of historical development. The very qualities which have made these commentato s excellent guides to an understanding of the theological treatises, render them unsuitable conductors on thay far older and quite differently cicumstanced domain. As the w-called clus cl Śansknt was perfocdy familiar to them, they sought its ordinary idicm in the Vedic hymes also. Since any difference in the ritual appeared to them inconceivable and the present forms were believed to have e)insd from the beginning of the world, they fancied that the parrivchs of the Indian religion must have sacri red in theavery sare manner. As the recŚgnized mytholegical and clasucal systems of their own age appeared ro them unassall bs and revealed verities, they must necessprily (se the commenta' 3 thu ght) be discoterable in that centre point of revelauSi, ths hymns of the ancient Rishis, who ad, indeed, lived in familiar in exourse with the ‘Gods, and possessed far higher wisdom tha: the succceding generations... It Is never occured do any o .e to make our understanding of the Hebrew books of the Old Testament depend on the Talmud and the Rabbins, while there are not wantingegcholars who hold it as the duty of a conscientious interpreter of the Veda to translate in conformity with Sâyaya, Mahtdhara, etc. Consequently, we do pt believe like H.H. Wilson, that Sâyaṇa, for instance, understood the expressions of the Veda better than any European interpreter ; but we think that a conscientious Luropean interpreter may understand the Veda far better and more correctly than Śâyana. We do not esteem it our first task to arrive at that understanding of the Veda which was current in India some centuries ago, but to search out the sense waich the poets themselves have put into their hymns and utterances. Hence we are of opinion that the writings of SŚâyana and the other commentators do not form a rule for the interpreter, but are merely one of those helps of which the latter will avail himsel: for the execution of his undoubtedly difficult ta-k, a task which is not to be asacomplished at the first onset, or by any single individual. ..We have, therefore, endeavoured to follaw the path grescribed by philology, to derive from the texs themselves the sense which they contain, by a juxtaposition of all the passages winch are cognate in diction or contents ;—a tedious and laborious path, in which ne'ther the commentators nor the translators have preceded us. The double duty of ex:gete ana lexicogrpher has thus devolved upon us. A simple etymological procedure, practised as it must be by those who seek to divine the sense of a word from the sole consideration of the passage before them without regard to the ten or twenty other passages in which it requrs, cannot possibly lead to a correct result," Professor Max Miller says : “As the authors of (the Brâh. manas were biinded "by thgology, the autheks of the still later Niruktas were deceived by etymological fictions, and both conspired to mislead by their authority later and more sensible commentators, such as Sâyana. Where Sâyana hae no authority. ta mislead him, his commentary is, at all events rational ; but still his scholastic notions would never allow him to g- cpt the fgg interpretation which comparative study gf these venerable documents forces ugon the unprejudiced scholar. We must therefore discover ourselves the real vettiges of these ancient poets.

Professor Benfey says : “Every one who has carefully studied the Indian interpretations is aware that absolutely no continuous tradition extending from the composition of the Veda to their explanation by Indian scholars, can be assumed ; that, on the 'contrary, between the genuine poetic remains of Vedic antiquity and their interpretations a long-continued break in tradition must have intervened, out of which at most the comprehension of some particulars may have been rescued and handed down to later times by means of liturgical usages and words, for.nule, and perhaps, also, poems connected therewith. Betides these remains of tradition, which must be estimated as very scanty, the interpreters of the Veda had, in the main, scarcely any other helps than those which, for the most part, are still at our command, the usage of the classical speech, and the grammatical and, etymological-lexicographical investigation of words. At the utmost, they found some aid in materials preserved il local dialects ; but this advantage is almost entirely outweighed by the comparison which we are able to institute with the Zend, and that which we can make (though here we must of course proceed with caution and prudence) with the languages cognate to the Sansknit,—a comparison which has already supplied so many helps to a clearer understanding of the Vedss. Bvt quite irrespectively of all particular aids, the Indian method of interpx tation becomes in its whole essence an entirely false one, owing to the prejudice with whith it chooses to conceive the ancient circumstances and ideas which have become quite strange to it, from its own religious stand-point, so many centuries mors receṅt, whilst, on the other hand, an advantage for the comprehension of the whole is secured to us by the — (drawn from analogous relations) with the life, the conceptions, the waits, of ancient peoples and popular songs, which we possess,—an advantage which, even if the Indians owed more details that they actually do owe, to tradition, would not be eclipsed by their interpretation. " aA very different opinion of the value of the Indian commentators was held and expressed by Professor Goldstiicker. “Without the vast information," he says, “which those commentators have disclosed to us,—without their method of explaining the obscurest text,—in one word, without their scholarship, we should still stand at the outer doors of Hindu antiquity." He ridicules the assertion that a European scholar can understand the Veda more correctly than Sâyaṇa, or arrive more nearly at the meaning which the Rishis gave to their own hymns, and yet even this stanch champion of the Indian commentators “cannot be altogether acquitted (as Dr. J. Muir says and shows) of a certain heretical tendency to deviate in practice from the interpretations of Śâyaṇa."

The last quotation which I shall make in connexion with this question is from Professor E. B. Cowell's Preface to his edition of Vol. V. of Wilson's Translation of the Rig-Feda Sanhitâ ; “This work does not preteritd to give a complete translation of the Rig-Veda, but only a faithful image of that particular phase of its interpretation which the medieval Hindus, as represented by SŚâyana, have preserved. This view is in itself interesting and of an historical value ; but far wider and deeper study is needed to pierce to the real meaning of these old hymns. SŚâyana's commentary will always retain a value of its own,—even its mistakes are often iReresting,—but his explanation mst nor for a moment bar the progress of scholarship. We can be thankful to him for any real help ; but let us not forget the debt which we owe to modern scholars, especially to those of Germany. The great 5t. Petersburg1 Dictionary is indeed a monument of triumphant eruditiqafand it has inaugurated a new era in the interpretation of the Rig Veda."

¹ My translation, Jthen, is pardy based on the commentary of Sâyaṇna, corrected and regulated bye rational probability, context, and intercomparison of similar words and passages. For constant and most valuable assistence in my labour I am deeply indebted to the works of many illustrious scholars, some depar:ed, and soc, n.ppily, su flourishirg. I ans thankful to Sâyaṇa, my first guide to the hymns of the Rigveda ; to my revered Master, Professor H. H. Wiison ; to Professors Roth, Bentey, Weber, Ludwig, Max Miller, Geassmann, and Monier Williams, and Dr. John Mur and Mr. Wallis. I have also constited, ard shall probably make more use nvarafter of, the works of M. Bereaigne and Dr. Oldenberg ; or can I omit to mention the Srebenzig Leder dis Rigveda by Gelder and Kaegi, Der Rigveda, by Kacy), and Hymns from the Regveda, by Professor Petzrson of Bombay, all of which I have read wish pleasure and profit.

But it must not be supposed that European students and interpreters of the Vega cliim anything like infallibility, completeness, or finality for the results to which their researches have led them. All modern scaolars will allow that many hymns arc dark as the darkest oracle, that, as Professor Max Miller says, there are whole verses which, as yer, yield no sense whatever, and words the meaning of which we can only guess. As in the interpretation of the more difficult books of the Old Testament and the, Homeric poems, sas in the explanation of the Veda complete success, if ever attainable, can be attained only by the labours of gencratins of stholars..

The Hymns are contpâsed in various metres jome of which aye exceedingly simple and others comparatively complex and elaborate, and two og more d'fferent metres are frequently found in the same Hymn ; bne Hymy, for ins:nce, in Book I. shows nine distinct varictics in the same number of verses. The verses

— e oc or star's consist of three or more—generally three or four— Pâdas,e semi-hemistichs or hnes, each of which contains eight, eleven, or twelve syllables sometimes, bat rarcly, five, and still less frequently four "or mors than twelve. As regards quantity the first syllables of the line are not stricily defined, but the last four are regular, the measure being iambic in the eight and twelve syllable verses and trecnaic in these of eleven syllables. Partly by way of saf guard apa'nst the besetting tempation to paraphrase and expand, and par. ly in the hope of preserving however imperfectly, something of the form of the Hymns, I have translated each verse by a verse syllabically commensurate with the original and generally divided into corresponding hemistichs.

The verses consisting of three or four ocrosyllabic lines are tolerably well represented by rhe common octo.yllabie or dimeter iambic merce winch I hav: emplaved. In other verses I fave not attempted to reproduce or imir te rhe rhythm or metre, of the ong )al : such a rak, sunposing its siticfactory completion to be possibiz, would require more ume and labour than I could spare for the purpo::. All that I have done, or tried to do, is ta show to some extent the orwiral form of the Hymmby rendering them mm syllabically commensurate hemistichs and verses, as Benfcy and the wanslutors of the Seventy Hymns have dene for a portion of the Rigveda, and Grassmann for nearly the whole of the Collection. o For further information regardiag the Rigveda the English reader is referred to Max Miillers History of Ancient Sanskrit Licrature, Muir's Original Sanskrit 7e)ts, and Weber's History of Indian Literature ;' or if asimpler antl more bopular exgosition be required, tq Mrs. Manning's India" Ancient and Media val, or to Kaegr's Der Rigveda, of which an English translation hes recently appeared. The student who reads. German and French will, as a matter of course, consult Ludwig's great work Der Rigveda and Bergaigne's Etudes sur la Religion Vâdique.

To conclude, my reasons for publishing this =. ork are chiefly these : there is at present no complete translation of the Rigveda in English, Professor "Wilson's version—of which the last two volumes have only lately apptared—bceing “only a faithful image of that particular phase of its interpretation which the mediaval Hindus, as represented by Sâyana, have preserved," and, moreover, the price of Wilson's six volumes —upwards of ninety rupces—purts the work beyond the reach of the great majority of readers in India.

I can hardly hope that my work will find acceptance with Pandits and Indian scholars inasmuch as I venture to deviate both widely and frequently from Śâyana whom they have been taught to regard as infallible. No arguments are likely to shake this belict. Nothing short of a course of study similar ta that to which tic leaders of the modern school of Vedic interpretation have devoted half their lives will enable them to see with our eyes and accept our views. I rust, however, thât they wall at any rate give the leaders and the followers of rhis modern school credir for deep devation to ancient Indian literature and due admiration of the great Indian scholars who have expounded i ; and will acknowledge that these modern scholars-—however mistaken their views may appear io be are labouring sincerely and solely to discover and declare the. spirit and the truth of the most ancient and veverat.d literary records thar are the heritage of Aryan man. KoravIR INUIGIRT Ś. T. H. GRIFFITH. May 251, 1689.

. NoTR.
